newsitem.title: GHANA: FEATURE-Ghana tastes American-style election razzamatazz.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Ghana tastes American-style election razzamatazz.

text.p: With multi-party presidential and legislative elections just weeks away, the political temperature in Ghana is rising.
Parties campaigning hard for the December 7 polls, the second since the restoration of democracy, hold rallies daily -- laced with American-style election razzamatazz.
The capital of the gold and cocoa producing West African country is fast disappearing behind giant billboards, posters and stickers as election fever takes hold.
Slick political slogans and advertising spots proliferate on state television.
But the threat of political violence, while only an isolated problem so far, is nonetheless real.
"Elections without violence strengthen Ghana's democracy," reads one bumper sticker widely distributed by the former British colony's National Electoral Commission.
Ghana's charismatic leader, Jerry Rawlings, 49, a rough-diamond two-time coup leader turned elected president, is seeking a final four-year term in the presidential poll.
Two main opposition parties, for once, have set aside past divisions and rivalry to launch a determined pitch for power.
But in a country with a tradition of settling communal or tribal chieftancy disputes violently, particularly upcountry, the cocktail is potentially explosive.
Tempers frayed in the north town of Tamale over the weekend of October 26 and rival groups clashed with home-made guns, stones and cutlasses, wounding several people, some seriously.

"It was mainly a clash between two youth gangs, the Uganda Boys and the Rwanda Boys," one senior resident told Reuters by telephone on condition of anonymity. "They are, so to speak, the thug-wings of the political parties here and made up of hardened youngsters working at the bus station as loaders," he said.
Apart from minor incidents -- and a well-publicised cabinet brawl between Rawlings and his then vice-president -- the last major political flare-up dates back to May 1995.

Five people were shot dead in Accra at an opposition protest against increased Value Added Tax. Witnesses blamed young men wearing T-shirts of the pro-Rawlings Committees for the Defence of the Revolution (CDR).
At the height of Rawlings's pre-democracy revolution in the mid-1980s, the CDRs arrested thousands of people for subversion and dispensed summary justice through People's Tribunals.
Pro-opposition newspapers say the committees -- officially disarmed -- still have weapons and are prepared to fight if Rawlings and his National Democratic Congress lose.
The opposition has never accepted Rawlings's 1992 presidential election win, dubbing it the "stolen victory".
The New Patriotic Party (NPP) and the People's Convention Party (PCP), against the odds, formed an alliance in August, and chose NPP's John Kufuor as a joint candidate.
Although there is a third candidate, surgeon Edward Mahama of the People's National Convention, most pundits agree the race is between Rawlings and Kufuor -- and is likely to be close.

Rawlings, an airforce flight-lieutenant who took power in 1979, restored civilian rule only to seize power again in 1981. He is a crowd-puller but, as he admitted in remarks after his December 1995 cabinet scuffle, he is "not much of a diplomat".
Kufuor, 57, is a seasoned politician, lawyer and businessman. He has sat in parliament and served briefly as a minister under Rawlings in 1982.
His party, which won almost a third of the vote in 1992, groups the professional classes with moderate conservative tradition.
The PCP, which did not exist in 1992, follows the socialist line promoted by Kwame Nkrumah, Ghana's first president.
Nkrumist parties won about 15 percent of the 1992 vote.

Rawlings is campaigning on his record. "The man has been at work for the past 15 years, everybody knows that he works towards turning Ghana into a middle-income country by the year 2020," his press secretary Vincent Asiseh says.

"Rawlings has tarred roads, but that is not what development is about. Development is bringing jobs, drinking water, schools and health facilities to the people," his PCP opposite number Kwabena Baffour says. Baffour, a former minister, fled Ghana after Rawlings' second coup.
Foreign diplomats, businessmen and other pundits predict Rawlings will win the presidential election with a strong opposition showing in the contest for parliament's 200 seats.
They predict only isolated pockets of political unrest.
The National Electoral Commission, which holds weekly inter-party meetings, enjoys the confidence of all sides.
The U.S. Development Agency USAID has spent $9 million over the past two years to revamp the NEC and train its 1,000 staff.

The European Union, Denmark, Germany, the Netherlands and other donors such as China have pitched in with transparent ballot boxes, radio communication equipment, computers and even hurricane lamps for vote-counting in the event of a power cut.
"We have no problem, no fears," says NEC chairman Kwadwo Afari-Gyan. "Together with all political parties we have been preparing these elections for years."
